newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Albright presses Vietnam on economic reforms, human rights.
newsitem.headline: Albright presses Vietnam on economic reforms, human rights.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Friday pressed Vietnam to speed up economic reforms and improve human rights, including release of political prisoners and greater freedoms of speech, assembly and religion.

But despite these concerns, she signed a copyright pact with the government and announced that she had authorised the U.S. trade and development agency to include Vietnam in its programmes. The agency gives grants for expensive feasibility studies to U.S. firms competing for large projects.

The United States is "disappointed with the pace of economic reforms," Albright told a news conference after her meetings with Vietnamese Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet and Foreign minister Nguyen Manh Cam.
She called for a Doi Moi 2, meaning a second phase of economic innovations.
Vietnam must remove barriers to trade and investment and create a legal framework for companies to operate, she said.

U.S. firms say Vietnam has been slow to enact the reforms needed to do business in the country and Hanoi has been pushing for most favoured nation trade benefits. It is one of only a half-dozen countries that does not have the status.

But Albright said Vietnam first has to speed issuing exit permits under a programme that aimed to encourage Vietnamese refugees in places like Thailand and Hong Kong to return home. The lure was a last chance to be considered for resettlement in the United States under liberal criteria.

Once Hanoi's cooperation improves, the Jackson-Vanik law, which demands free immigration in return for trade ties, can be waived and American firms can qualify for government loans and insurance to do business in Vietnam, Albright said.
She said she could recommend that Jackson-Vanik be waived soon, if the visa processing is accelerated.
Also, once this is followed by a trade agreement, Vietnam can qualify for most favoured nation benefits, which Hanoi is keen to have.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Vietnamese officials pledged their commitment to economic reforms.

On human rights, a sensitive issue with Hanoi, Albright raised the specific cases of three political prisoners and stressed the need for Vietnam to allow greater freedoms of speech, religion and assembly.
The cases involved political dissidents Doan Viet Hoat and Nguyen Van Que and Buddhist leader Thich Quang Do.
Albright handed Cam a letter from Hoat's wife and asked him to ensure the letter was delivered and to allow the wife, who is now in the United States, to visit her husband.

Burns said Cam accepted the letter without comment but Kiet made the case with Albright that the two countries have a different approach to human rights and Vietnam must be concerned about internal stability.
Albright also said she pressed Hanoi to assign more personnel to the U.S. search for American servicemen missing from the Vietnam War. Burns said Kiet pledged full cooperation.
Albright, on her first visit to Vietnam as secretary of state, arrived in Hanoi stressing her intention to press Vietnamese leaders on the need for speedier economic reforms.

But her first act on Friday was to be briefed by military officer overseeing the U.S. missing-in-action office that searches for the 1,584 servicemen in Vietnam still unaccounted for after the war that the Americans lost in 1975.
Of that number, 196 were priority cases in January 1992 -- that is, cases based on live sightings of individuals -- and now only 48 individuals remain on that list, military officials said.
The issue has long been an emotional one in the United States, which for years was bitterly rent by the war in which it backed South Vietnam against the communist North.
But there are increasing suggestions the intense search for missing servicemen -- costing about $10 million a year -- may one day have to end without resolving all the cases.
"I don't think you'll get 100 percent accounting," said Army Lt. Col. Jonathan Chase, the chief of the search operations who briefed Albright.

Albright told reporters: "I think that for thousands of Americans the POW-MIA situation will never be resolved. It will clearly be part of the agenda and it will clearly be part of a priority issue that we keep pressing."

Nevertheless, with Vietnam viewed as a key regional economic player and regional political power, she said: "I think people know the importance that has to be attached to dealing with Vietnam as a country."
